articles.title: Scientists who discovered a third form of magnetism win major physics prize
articles.summary: Physicists have uncovered a hidden third form of magnetism that challenges more than 100 years of established physics. Called altermagnetism, the discovery could transform future computing and electronics while opening an entirely new frontier in quantum research.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown form of magnetism, overturning an understanding of magnetic behavior that had stood for more than a century. The discovery, known as altermagnetism, has revealed a third fundamental category of collinear magnetism and opened new possibilities for quantum materials, advanced electronics, and future computing technologies.

Three physicists responsible for the breakthrough have been named recipients of the 2026 Europhysics Prize, one of Europe's most prestigious honors in condensed matter physics. The European Physical Society (EPS) Condensed Matter Division selected Professor Jairo Sinova of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), Dr. Libor Šmejkal, and Professor Tomas Jungwirth for their work establishing altermagnetism as a distinct form of magnetic order alongside ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

"This award recognizes a fundamental discovery that challenged one of the most established paradigms in condensed matter physics," said Professor Jairo Sinova, Director of the Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center (SPICE) at Mainz University. "Discovering that an entirely new magnetic phase had remained hidden for more than one hundred years demonstrates that even the most mature scientific fields can still hold fundamental surprises."

The breakthrough emerged from years of collaboration between Sinova's research group at Mainz University and Jungwirth's team at the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences in Prague. Šmejkal, who also maintained an affiliation in Prague, spent eight years at Mainz between 2016 and 2024, first pursuing doctoral research and later working as a postdoctoral scientist in Sinova's group.

During that period, Šmejkal played a leading role in developing the theoretical framework behind altermagnetism. By combining advanced mathematical approaches to symmetry with spintronics, which studies how electron spin can be used in electronic devices, the researchers identified a previously unrecognized pattern of magnetic behavior.

Their predictions soon attracted experimental teams around the world. Measurements of electronic properties and electrical transport in multiple materials provided evidence supporting the new magnetic classification. Altermagnetism has since grown into one of the most active areas of condensed matter physics, with research efforts expanding across Europe, North America, and Asia.

A Third Form of Magnetism Rewrites Physics

For more than 100 years, physicists generally divided collinear magnets into two fundamental categories: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets.

Ferromagnets have an overall magnetic alignment that produces a net magnetization. These materials are essential to many magnetic memory technologies used today. In conventional antiferromagnets, opposing magnetic moments cancel one another, leaving no overall magnetization and producing electronic behavior very different from that of ferromagnets.

Altermagnetism introduces a surprising third possibility.

Like antiferromagnets, altermagnets have magnetic moments that cancel out, resulting in no net magnetization. However, their electrons can exhibit properties previously associated with ferromagnets.

This unusual combination allows altermagnets to support electrical currents with strongly polarized electron spins while also displaying extremely rapid magnetic dynamics. Those characteristics could make them valuable for a new generation of spintronic devices, potentially advancing the speed and capabilities of future information technologies.

The significance extends well beyond electronics. Altermagnetism represents a previously unrecognized symmetry class of matter and has revealed unexpected connections to several major areas of modern physics, including topological phenomena, unconventional superconductivity, and quantum materials with strong interactions between electrons.

How Scientists Discovered Altermagnetism

The path toward this discovery began with theoretical investigations into unusual ways that electricity moves through magnetic materials. Among the early advances was the prediction of the crystal anomalous Hall effect, a phenomenon involving electrical transport in certain crystal structures.

Initially, these unexpected behaviors might have appeared to be unusual features of individual materials. However, the researchers eventually recognized that they were connected by a broader principle involving symmetries of electron spins.

Rather than representing isolated exceptions to established magnetic behavior, these materials belonged to an entirely different magnetic category.

A major milestone came in 2022, when the team published a comprehensive symmetry classification of altermagnetism and identified hundreds of materials that could potentially exhibit it.

Experimental physicists subsequently tested these predictions using several complementary methods. These included angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), which reveals how electrons behave inside materials, along with measurements of electrical transport.

The results confirmed altermagnetic behavior in several materials, helping establish the new classification experimentally.

Interest in the discovery has expanded rapidly. Hundreds of scientific papers have appeared within just a few years, and altermagnetism has become a prominent subject at international physics conferences. The growing research community is now investigating both its fundamental properties and its potential technological applications.

Discovery Earns Prestigious 2026 Europhysics Prize

The Europhysics Prize recognizes major advances in condensed matter physics, a field concerned with the physical properties and behavior of materials. Established in 1975, the award honors discoveries that have significantly advanced scientific understanding, with a substantial share of the recognized research conducted in Europe.

The 2026 prize recognizes the theoretical and experimental advances that established altermagnetism as a new fundamental form of collinear magnetic order.

The award ceremony was scheduled for September 2026 at the 32nd General Conference of the European Physical Society Condensed Matter Division (CMD32) in Graz, Austria.

The Scientists Behind the Breakthrough

Professor Jairo Sinova is a physics professor at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany and director of the university's Spin Phenomena Interdisciplinary Center. His research investigates magnetism, spintronics, and quantum materials.

Dr. Libor Šmejkal conducted much of the crucial theoretical work that led to the identification of altermagnetism while working at Mainz University from 2016 to 2024. His current affiliations include the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids, and the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Professor Tomas Jungwirth is affiliated with the Institute of Physics of the Czech Academy of Sciences and the University of Nottingham. He has collaborated extensively with Sinova's Mainz research team and played a central role in establishing the theoretical foundations of altermagnetism.

Together, their work has revealed a fundamental property of magnetic matter that escaped recognition for more than a century, opening an entirely new direction for research into quantum physics and future electronic technologies.

articles.personality_title: Scientists discover a new form of magnetism, winning a major physics prize
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For over 100 years, scientists believed there were only two types of magnetism in materials: ferromagnetism, which creates a magnetic field like a fridge magnet, and antiferromagnetism, where magnetic forces cancel out. These ideas shaped much of our understanding of magnets and their use in technology.

**What happened** – A team of three physicists—Professor Jairo Sinova, Dr. Libor Šmejkal, and Professor Tomas Jungwirth—discovered a third kind of magnetism called altermagnetism. They worked together over many years, combining math and experiments to prove this new magnetic behavior exists. Their discovery shows that some materials have magnetic properties that don’t fit into the old two categories. For this work, they won the prestigious 2026 Europhysics Prize.

**Impact** – Altermagnetism is special because it mixes features of the two known types of magnetism. Like antiferromagnets, it has no overall magnetic field, but like ferromagnets, it can control the spin of electrons, which is important for new electronics called spintronics. This could help make faster and more efficient computers and devices. The discovery also changes how scientists think about magnets and opens new research paths in physics.

**What's next step** – Researchers around the world are now studying altermagnetism to understand it better and find materials that use it. This work could lead to new technologies in computing and electronics. Scientists will also explore how this new magnetic behavior connects to other physics fields, like superconductivity and quantum materials.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have found a new kind of magnetism, altermagnetism, that challenges old ideas and could lead to advances in future electronics and physics research.

articles.title: Physicists create a bizarre new quantum state called a fractional fermi sea
articles.summary: Physicists have discovered a strange new state of quantum matter in which ultracold atoms defy familiar organizational rules, forming a highly excited yet surprisingly orderly configuration called a "fractional Fermi sea." The discovery challenges established quantum theories and hints at exotic quasiparticles that scientists have dubbed potential "super-Fermions."
articles.content:
Physicists have uncovered a strange new form of quantum behavior in which particles organize themselves in ways that challenge established theories. Even more surprising, the particles maintain a remarkable hidden order despite being driven into an extremely energetic state.

In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers from the group led by Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, working with theoretical physicist Alvise Bastianello of the CNRS and Université Paris-Dauphine, describe how to engineer an exotic quantum state known as a "fractional Fermi sea."

The breakthrough involves pushing ultracold cesium atoms far beyond their normal conditions by repeatedly changing how strongly they attract or repel one another. Rather than simply becoming disordered, the particles rearrange themselves into an unusual configuration that behaves differently from the quantum systems scientists have traditionally studied.

The theoretical findings provide the foundation for recent experimental research conducted by Nägerl's team at the Department of Experimental Physics.

Pushing Quantum Particles Beyond Their Normal Limits

Under ordinary conditions, quantum particles follow well-established rules that determine how they arrange themselves, particularly at extremely low temperatures.

One important example involves fermions, a category of particles that includes electrons. These particles cannot all occupy the same quantum state, so they fill available energy levels according to specific restrictions. At very low temperatures, this arrangement produces what physicists call a Fermi sea.

But what happens when researchers deliberately disrupt the conditions that normally govern how particles behave?

As Alvise Bastianello explains: "Fermions, for instance, stack neatly into the available energy states to form the so-called 'Fermi sea'. But what happens if one forces interacting atoms to continuously cycle through extreme conditions, smoothly shifting them from strongly repelling each other to strongly attracting each other?"

To investigate this possibility, the researchers studied ultracold cesium atoms confined to a one-dimensional system. This means the atoms are restricted to moving along a single direction, creating an environment in which their quantum interactions can be studied with exceptional control.

The team examined what happens when the interactions between these atoms are repeatedly adjusted, cycling between powerful repulsion and attraction.

Their calculations revealed something unexpected. Starting from the ground state, the lowest energy configuration available to the system, the atoms could be driven into a highly excited state without losing their underlying organization.

The researchers call this unusual arrangement a fractional Fermi sea because its particles appear to obey a modified rule governing how quantum states are occupied.

"Instead of simply heating the system, the interaction cycle reorganizes the atoms into a new many-body state," says Yi Zeng, the leading author of this study. "This gives us a controlled way to explore quantum matter beyond the usual equilibrium paradigms."

A Strange New Quantum State With Hidden Order

One of the most intriguing features of the fractional Fermi sea is that its particles remain organized even though the system has been pushed far from equilibrium.

In physics, equilibrium describes a condition in which a system's overall properties have settled into a stable balance. Systems driven far from equilibrium can behave in complicated and unexpected ways, making them particularly challenging to understand.

Yet the fractional Fermi sea is not simply a collection of excited particles behaving randomly. Instead, it contains distinctive mathematical patterns that reveal a deeper structure.

Among these patterns are pronounced ripples called Friedel oscillations. These are wave-like variations associated with the way quantum particles influence one another. The researchers also identified unusual patterns in how correlations between particles weaken with increasing distance, even when the repulsive interactions are relatively weak.

These signatures are important because they differ from predictions associated with Tomonaga-Luttinger liquid theory, a long-established framework for describing how interacting quantum particles behave in one-dimensional systems.

The findings therefore point toward a previously unexplored type of quantum behavior that cannot be fully described using this familiar theoretical picture.

"This state is highly excited, but it is not random," says Hanns-Christoph Nägerl, the group leader. "It has a hidden order that becomes visible in its correlations."

The strange behavior also raises questions about the effective particles that emerge within the system. Physicists call these collective excitations quasiparticles because they can behave like individual particles even though they arise from the coordinated motion of many interacting particles.

Nägerl suggests that the unusual excitations might eventually deserve a name of their own.

"We are not yet sure how we should name these new quasiparticles. Perhaps 'super-Fermions'?"

Opening a New Frontier in Quantum Physics

The discovery suggests that fractional Fermi seas represent an exotic critical phase of quantum matter, with characteristic patterns of particle correlations that extend beyond existing descriptions of one-dimensional quantum systems.

It also demonstrates the growing power of quantum simulation, a technique that allows scientists to use carefully controlled quantum systems to investigate physical behavior that would otherwise be difficult to reproduce or study.

Ultracold atoms are particularly useful for this purpose because researchers can precisely adjust their interactions and observe how the resulting quantum states change.

Rather than limiting these experiments to recreating phenomena already understood through established theories, scientists can now explore deliberately engineered states that reveal entirely new possibilities.

As Hanns-Christoph Nägerl says: "The discovery of fractional Fermi seas shows how far we can push quantum simulation: not only reproducing known models, but creating and probing states that go beyond established paradigms."

The current publication establishes the theoretical framework for fractional Fermi seas. A companion study describing their experimental realization through quantum simulation is undergoing peer review.

Together, the research points toward new ways of investigating the fundamental behavior of quantum matter, including unusual collective excitations and hidden forms of order that emerge only when particles are pushed far outside their normal conditions.

This discovery challenges existing theories and opens new research frontiers in quantum matter, with broad implications for fundamental physics and quantum simulation technology. The article provides detailed context and explains the experimental and theoretical advances, demonstrating a meaningful positive impact on scientific understanding.

articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent un nouvel état quantique appelé mer de Fermi fractionnaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les physiciens étudient depuis longtemps comment de petites particules appelées fermions, comme les électrons, s’organisent à très basse température. Ces particules suivent généralement des règles strictes, remplissant des niveaux d’énergie pour former ce qu’on appelle une mer de Fermi. Comprendre ces arrangements aide à mieux connaître le comportement de la matière à très petite échelle.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe dirigée par Hanns-Christoph Nägerl et Alvise Bastianello a découvert un nouvel état quantique en expérimentant avec des atomes de césium ultrafroids. Ils ont modifié à plusieurs reprises la force avec laquelle ces atomes s’attirent ou se repoussent, tout en les confinant à se déplacer sur une seule ligne. Au lieu de devenir désordonnés, les atomes ont formé un motif surprenant appelé mer de Fermi fractionnaire, qui se comporte différemment de tout ce qui avait été vu auparavant.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car elle montre que les particules peuvent rester organisées même lorsqu’elles sont poussées dans des conditions très énergiques et inhabituelles, rompant avec les règles habituelles. Ce nouvel état présente des motifs cachés et des interactions inhabituelles entre particules qui défient les théories existantes sur les systèmes quantiques unidimensionnels. Il suggère aussi l’existence de nouveaux quasiparticules, que les chercheurs proposent d’appeler « super-fermions ».

**Prochaine étape** – L’équipe continue d’étudier cette mer de Fermi fractionnaire par des expériences et des calculs théoriques. Leur objectif est de mieux comprendre ces nouvelles quasiparticules et d’explorer comment cette découverte peut aider à révéler d’autres comportements quantiques inconnus. Cela pourrait faire avancer la simulation quantique, une technique pour étudier la physique complexe en contrôlant de petites particules.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des physiciens ont créé et étudié un nouvel état quantique, la mer de Fermi fractionnaire, révélant un ordre inattendu chez des particules poussées au-delà de leurs conditions normales et ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour la recherche quantique.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren un nuevo estado cuántico llamado mar de Fermi fraccional
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los físicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo cómo las pequeñas partículas llamadas fermiones, como los electrones, se organizan a temperaturas muy bajas. Estas partículas suelen seguir reglas estrictas, llenando niveles de energía para formar lo que se llama un mar de Fermi. Entender estas organizaciones ayuda a aprender sobre el comportamiento de la materia en las escalas más pequeñas.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo dirigido por Hanns-Christoph Nägerl y Alvise Bastianello encontró un nuevo y extraño estado cuántico al experimentar con átomos de cesio ultrafríos. Cambiaron repetidamente la fuerza con la que estos átomos se atraen o repelen mientras los mantenían confinados para moverse en una sola línea. En lugar de desordenarse, los átomos formaron un patrón sorprendente llamado mar de Fermi fraccional, que se comporta de manera diferente a todo lo visto antes.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque muestra que las partículas pueden mantenerse organizadas incluso cuando se llevan a condiciones muy energéticas e inusuales, rompiendo las reglas normales que los científicos esperaban. El nuevo estado tiene patrones ocultos e interacciones poco comunes entre partículas que desafían las teorías existentes sobre sistemas cuánticos unidimensionales. También sugiere nuevos tipos de cuasipartículas, que los investigadores llaman "super-Fermiones".

**Próximo paso** – El equipo sigue estudiando este mar de Fermi fraccional mediante experimentos y teoría. Su objetivo es comprender mejor estas nuevas cuasipartículas y ver cómo este descubrimiento puede ayudar a explorar otros comportamientos cuánticos desconocidos. Esto podría llevar a avances en la simulación cuántica, una técnica para estudiar física compleja controlando partículas muy pequeñas.

**Frase clave** – Los físicos han creado y estudiado un nuevo estado cuántico llamado mar de Fermi fraccional, revelando un orden inesperado en partículas llevadas más allá de sus condiciones normales y abriendo nuevos caminos para la investigación cuántica.

articles.title: How to compare and strengthen research systems
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03309-3Analysing national research systems by using open-access data and new methods can help countries to learn from each other.
articles.content:
How does a country get the biggest bang for its buck when it comes to science? Comparing science systems between countries can be a good way to see what’s working well and what’s not. But it’s difficult to do.

Want to speed up scientific progress? First understand how science policy works

Different countries analyse different things; relevant data can be hard to find or access; and the same concepts can be defined and measured in various ways.

Scientific outputs such as numbers of publications, citations and patents are easy to quantify. But they say little about what factors influenced them. Standardized statistics published by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), for example on investments, allow for easy comparisons between countries. But these measurements are not enough to analyse the intertwined effects that different approaches to funding, running institutions and supporting researchers can have over time. Some metrics — such as how funding shapes researchers’ careers — are rarely measured systematically.

And even when countries report on similar measures, differences in data collection can make comparisons difficult. For example, one country reporting information about its fundamental research might publish detailed spending statistics by sector and funding source; another might report only aggregated spending that includes applied research. This makes it hard to form a coherent global picture.

To overcome these problems, a group that I lead has developed an approach to analysing national research systems — gathering data from a broad range of sources and developing measures for often-overlooked aspects of such systems. I hope that other researchers, funders and international organizations will use our framework, and find ways to improve it.

China’s shift towards ‘organized research’: how can coordination and innovation co-exist?

Our project, the China Fundamental Research Report, examines research systems in 25 countries and regions, including the European Union (www.cfrr.net). The chosen regions have systems of various sizes, structures and stages of development. In particular, China offers a useful case study because its scientific landscape has transformed over the past 40 years, through sustained investment in funding, institutions, talent and research infrastructure.

Our work was possible thanks to a rapid expansion in the amount of research information that is now openly available — from publication and funding databases to data repositories and more. This has made it much easier to compare many facets of research between countries. We used large-scale computational methods to analyse data sets that were previously difficult to study together.

One key part of our work was developing fresh indicators to capture areas of research that are not usually measured. For example, we used large language models to identify signals of novelty in research questions and methods — how far a study ventures beyond established knowledge. We also linked publications to patent citations to trace connections between fundamental research and technological development. And we combined funding and workforce data to trace how, in China, junior researchers make a substantial contribution to scientific output. This group, we found, was supported by a long-term expansion of funding for early-career researchers from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a meaningful advancement in analyzing and comparing national research systems using open-access data and new computational methods. This approach has broad significance as it can help countries learn from each other to improve science policy and accelerate scientific progress globally. The focus on developing new indicators and leveraging large-scale data to better understand research impact and funding effectiveness provides substantial context and substance.
articles.personality_title: New methods help countries compare and improve their science systems
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Countries want to know how to get the best results from their investments in science. Comparing how different nations support research can show what works well and what could be better. But this is hard because countries collect and report data in different ways.

**What happened** – A research team created a new way to study national science systems using open data and advanced computer tools. They looked at 25 countries, including China, to measure not just usual statistics like publications and patents, but also new factors like how early-career scientists are supported and how research connects to technology. They used methods like large language models to detect new ideas in research.

**Impact** – This approach gives a clearer and deeper picture of how countries run their science programs. For example, it showed how China’s long-term funding for young researchers helped boost scientific output. By comparing many details, countries can learn from each other’s successes and challenges in science policy.

**What's next step** – The researchers hope others will use and improve their system to analyze research worldwide. This could lead to better decisions about funding, supporting scientists, and encouraging innovation in many countries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New tools and open data now let countries compare their science systems more fairly and learn how to support research better for faster progress.

**Contexto** – Los países quieren saber cómo obtener los mejores resultados de sus inversiones en ciencia. Analizaron 25 países, incluida China, para medir no solo estadísticas comunes como publicaciones y patentes, sino también nuevos factores como el apoyo a científicos jóvenes y cómo la investigación se conecta con la tecnología. Usaron modelos de lenguaje para detectar ideas nuevas en la investigación.
